1.pericope_label: And David assembled all the princes of Israel, the princes of the tribes, and the captains of the companies that ministered to the king by course, and the captains over the thousands, and captains over the hundreds, and the stewards over all the substance and possession of the king, and of his sons, with the officers, and with the mighty men, and with all the valiant men, unto Jerusalem. Then David the king stood up upon his feet, and said, Hear me, my brethren, and my people: As for me, I had in mine heart to build an house of rest for the ark of the covenant of the Lord, and for the footstool of our God, and had made ready for the building:

schools.summary: Read the gathering as a formal transfer of office: Delitzsch lists its business in order, and both he and Ellicott take David's rising as rising from the throne, Delitzsch expressly denying he had been lying in bed.
Gill declines to choose between the couch and the throne, offering both and supporting the throne by an ancient custom under which even kings stood to address a crowd.
Clarke has David chiefly confined to his bed, receiving strength to rise only when the nobles came before him.
Henry frames the chapter as a dying king's last service to God and his country, and has David rise twice, first from the bed to meet them and then from his chair to speak.

debates.question: Was David rising from a sickbed or from his throne?

positions.position: From his bed, having received strength for the occasion
From the throne; he had been sitting, not lying
Both, in sequence: from the bed to meet them, then from the chair to speak
Either is possible; the ancients stood to address a crowd

debates.question: What does the address my brethren and my people express?

positions.position: Condescending goodwill, a king stooping to his subjects
Not condescension but acknowledgment that all Israel were kin and David the head of the family

outliers.claim: Cites the wounded Agamemnon, who would not speak sitting until he had excused himself for it, as pagan evidence for the custom of standing to address an assembly.

themes: And David assembled all the princes of Israel, the princes of the tribes, and the captains of the companies that ministered to the king by course, and the captains over the thousands, and captains over the hundreds, and the stewards over all the substance and possession of the king, and of his sons, with the officers, and with the mighty men, and with all the valiant men, unto Jerusalem.

Then David the king stood up upon his feet, and said, Hear me, my brethren, and my people: As for me, I had in mine heart to build an house of rest for the ark of the covenant of the Lord, and for the footstool of our God, and had made ready for the building:

3.pericope_label: But God said unto me, Thou shalt not build an house for my name, because thou hast been a man of war, and hast shed blood. Howbeit the Lord God of Israel chose me before all the house of my father to be king over Israel for ever: for he hath chosen Judah to be the ruler; and of the house of Judah, the house of my father; and among the sons of my father he liked me to make me king over all Israel: And of all my sons, (for the Lord hath given me many sons,) he hath chosen Solomon my son to sit upon the throne of the kingdom of the Lord over Israel.

schools.summary: Ellicott puts the stress on God in contrast with the I of the preceding clause, presses he liked me into it was I in whom He took pleasure, and calls the throne of the kingdom of the Lord unique in the Old Testament; Delitzsch identifies the footstool with the covering of the ark and notes the speech repeats in public what David had said privately to his son.
Gill supplies Nathan as the channel of the refusal, notes the choice of David passed over his elder brothers, and takes for ever by stages, from David's lifetime to his posterity to his antitype.
Clarke makes the perpetuity conditional for the dynasty but unconditional as the promise refers to Christ.

debates.question: How far does for ever reach in the promise to David?

positions.position: By stages: David's lifetime, then his posterity, and best of all his antitype
Conditional on obedience for the dynasty, without end as it refers to Christ

outliers.claim: Observes that David uses of himself the very phrase the voice from heaven spoke of the Son of David at his baptism, and that the throne of the kingdom of the Lord is an expression found nowhere else in the Old Testament, making the monarchy a vicegerency.

themes: But God said unto me, Thou shalt not build an house for my name, because thou hast been a man of war, and hast shed blood.

Howbeit the Lord God of Israel chose me before all the house of my father to be king over Israel for ever: for he hath chosen Judah to be the ruler; and of the house of Judah, the house of my father; and among the sons of my father he liked me to make me king over all Israel:
And of all my sons, (for the Lord hath given me many sons,) he hath chosen Solomon my son to sit upon the throne of the kingdom of the Lord over Israel.

6.pericope_label: And he said unto me, Solomon thy son, he shall build my house and my courts: for I have chosen him to be my son, and I will be his father. Moreover I will establish his kingdom for ever, if he be constant to do my commandments and my judgments, as at this day. Now therefore in the sight of all Israel the congregation of the Lord, and in the audience of our God, keep and seek for all the commandments of the Lord your God: that ye may possess this good land, and leave it for an inheritance for your children after you for ever.

schools.summary: Ellicott finds the emphatic pronoun, he and not thou, in the building commission and the doubled pronoun in the adoption clause, glosses as at this day as our present work, and reads the charge to the people as a formal adjuration modelled on Moses calling heaven and earth to witness.

Wesley makes Solomon a figure of the coming one who is both founder and foundation of the gospel temple, divides the promise into absolute for the Messiah and conditional for Solomon, and turns keep and seek into a program of obedience and study; Clarke records the Targum reading, Before the Word of the Lord.

debates.question: What does as at this day point to?

positions.position: As we are doing in our present work, the assembly's own labour
As Solomon hath begun, the young king's own start

debates.question: What is asked in the command to seek the commandments?

positions.position: Do not neglect them; resort to them always as the rule of right living
Keep what you know and search into what you are still ignorant of

outliers.claim: Divides the promise itself rather than its condition: absolute with regard to the Messiah, conditional with regard to Solomon.

themes: And he said unto me, Solomon thy son, he shall build my house and my courts: for I have chosen him to be my son, and I will be his father.
Moreover I will establish his kingdom for ever, if he be constant to do my commandments and my judgments, as at this day.

Now therefore in the sight of all Israel the congregation of the Lord, and in the audience of our God, keep and seek for all the commandments of the Lord your God: that ye may possess this good land, and leave it for an inheritance for your children after you for ever.

9.pericope_label: And thou, Solomon my son, know thou the God of thy father, and serve him with a perfect heart and with a willing mind: for the Lord searcheth all hearts, and understandeth all the imaginations of the thoughts: if thou seek him, he will be found of thee; but if thou forsake him, he will cast thee off for ever. Take heed now; for the Lord hath chosen thee to build an house for the sanctuary: be strong, and do it.

schools.summary: Ellicott narrows the God of thy father to the God of David on the strength of David's later my God, glosses the perfect heart as whole and unimpaired rather than flawless, links searcheth to the seek of the previous verse, and shows that cast thee off translates a strong word meaning to reject as foul-smelling.
Gill marks the turn from the assembly to the heir and offers two senses of take heed now without choosing between them.
Wesley makes knowing imply affection and practice, turns the searching of hearts directly on Solomon's possible pretence, and measures the threat by the promises and honours it would cancel.

debates.question: Is take heed now a warning or an introduction?

positions.position: A warning against forsaking God, or else simply a call to attend to what follows
See now that the Lord hath chosen thee: a commission to weigh and then act on

outliers.claim: Balances the condition by insisting that divine grace is not restricted even by it, seeking in earnest always ending in finding.

themes: And thou, Solomon my son, know thou the God of thy father, and serve him with a perfect heart and with a willing mind: for the Lord searcheth all hearts, and understandeth all the imaginations of the thoughts: if thou seek him, he will be found of thee; but if thou forsake him, he will cast thee off for ever.
Take heed now; for the Lord hath chosen thee to build an house for the sanctuary: be strong, and do it.

11.pericope_label: Then David gave to Solomon his son the pattern of the porch, and of the houses thereof, and of the treasuries thereof, and of the upper chambers thereof, and of the inner parlours thereof, and of the place of the mercy seat, And the pattern of all that he had by the spirit, of the courts of the house of the Lord, and of all the chambers round about, of the treasuries of the house of God, and of the treasuries of the dedicated things: Also for the courses of the priests and the Levites, and for all the work of the service of the house of the Lord, and for all the vessels of service in the house of the Lord.

schools.summary: Ellicott and Delitzsch both trace the description from outer to inner; Ellicott identifies the two houses as nave and chancel, the inner parlours as vestibule and holy place, does the arithmetic on the upper chambers, and follows Gesenius in deriving the treasury word from Semitic into Persian, while Delitzsch and Ellicott both attach the courses clause to the chambers round about rather than making it a new list.
Gill cites the Targum for the spirit of prophecy and records the Jewish tradition that Samuel was let into the design first and passed it to David.

Clarke describes what was handed over as a full architectural set with elevations and sections, and passes on Parkhurst's derivation of the treasury word from a verb meaning to treasure up and an adjective meaning pure; Wesley makes the inner parlours the side chambers built against the wall.

Henry argues that the model was necessary because no one had seen such a building, was given in writing or impressed as clearly as writing, and could not be left to David's devotion or Solomon's wisdom since the house was a kind of sacrament.

positions.position: The vestibule and the holy place, set against the inmost shrine
The side rooms built against the wall of the house round about

debates.question: Did the treasury word pass from Persian into Hebrew or the reverse?

positions.position: Persian into Hebrew; the related word means granary or hidden treasure
Semitic into Persian, following Gesenius, though the form here may be a late borrowing back

outliers.claim: Records a Jewish tradition that Samuel received the temple design first and delivered it to David.

themes: Then David gave to Solomon his son the pattern of the porch, and of the houses thereof, and of the treasuries thereof, and of the upper chambers thereof, and of the inner parlours thereof, and of the place of the mercy seat,

And the pattern of all that he had by the spirit, of the courts of the house of the Lord, and of all the chambers round about, of the treasuries of the house of God, and of the treasuries of the dedicated things:
Also for the courses of the priests and the Levites, and for all the work of the service of the house of the Lord, and for all the vessels of service in the house of the Lord.

14.pericope_label: He gave of gold by weight for things of gold, for all instruments of all manner of service; silver also for all instruments of silver by weight, for all instruments of every kind of service: Even the weight for the candlesticks of gold, and for their lamps of gold, by weight for every candlestick, and for the lamps thereof: and for the candlesticks of silver by weight, both for the candlestick, and also for the lamps thereof, according to the use of every candlestick. And by weight he gave gold for the tables of shewbread, for every table; and likewise silver for the tables of silver:

schools.summary: Ellicott reconstructs the concise Hebrew as a schedule of vessels with a weight specified against each, notes that the silver lampstands and silver tables are named nowhere else in the Old Testament, and conjectures that shewbread in the plural phrase is a gloss displacing the word gold.

Gill grounds the weights in the direction of the Spirit and supplies the Jewish reckoning, ten lampstands set five on each side of the older Mosaic one at a hundred pounds of gold apiece, and ten tables where the tabernacle had one.

Clarke states the contrast between one lampstand in the tabernacle and ten in the temple; Wesley distinguishes fixed from portable lampstands and harmonises the plural tables by making one of them pre-eminent.

debates.question: What does according to the use of every candlestick distinguish?

positions.position: The service each lampstand was to perform, a measurement clause
Lampstands fixed in place from those meant to be carried

debates.question: Why does the verse speak of tables of shewbread in the plural when the law knows only one?

positions.position: Because Solomon's temple had ten tables where the tabernacle had one
Because divers tables were used about the shewbread, one being of more eminency
Because shewbread is a gloss which displaced the word gold; the original read tables of gold

outliers.claim: Proposes a textual conjecture, that the word shewbread has displaced the word gold, which would fold the single shewbread table in among the ten golden ones.

themes: He gave of gold by weight for things of gold, for all instruments of all manner of service; silver also for all instruments of silver by weight, for all instruments of every kind of service:

Even the weight for the candlesticks of gold, and for their lamps of gold, by weight for every candlestick, and for the lamps thereof: and for the candlesticks of silver by weight, both for the candlestick, and also for the lamps thereof, according to the use of every candlestick.
And by weight he gave gold for the tables of shewbread, for every table; and likewise silver for the tables of silver:

17.pericope_label: Also pure gold for the fleshhooks, and the bowls, and the cups: and for the golden basons he gave gold by weight for every bason; and likewise silver by weight for every bason of silver: And for the altar of incense refined gold by weight; and gold for the pattern of the chariot of the cherubims, that spread out their wings, and covered the ark of the covenant of the Lord. All this, said David, the Lord made me understand in writing by his hand upon me, even all the works of this pattern.

schools.summary: Ellicott renders the last vessels as an inventory entry and assigns each its office, and both he and Delitzsch identify the chariot with the two figures on the covering of the ark, Delitzsch arguing from apposition that the cherubim and not the ark form the chariot; on the writing both worry at the grammar, Ellicott ending in a suspicion of corruption and Delitzsch attaching upon me to the writing rather than to the hand.
Gill explains the fleshhooks by their use and lays out the options for how the plan reached David, preferring a handwriting from the Lord delivered by angels, as the two tables were.

Wesley makes the refined gold of the incense altar typical of Christ's intercession, denies that the chariot means the cherubim Moses made, and draws from the word chariot the hint that God was not fixed to the house; Clarke prefers a vision of ecstasy and supplies the Targum's flattened rendering.

debates.question: Which cherubim are called the chariot, and what did they cover?

positions.position: The two figures on the covering of the ark, since God is said to ride upon a cherub
The larger pair Solomon was still to make; and they covered the ark before it, not above it

debates.question: How did the written pattern reach David?

positions.position: A handwriting from the Lord delivered by angels, as the two tables were
A vision of ecstasy impressed deeply enough to be described afterwards
Through a man of God who wrote it down, or written by God on the table of David's mind
Either by one of David's seers or from the older description of the Mosaic sanctuary; the text may be corrupt

outliers.claim: Quotes Delaney for the claim that Greek architecture descends from the temple design as from its fountain.

themes: Also pure gold for the fleshhooks, and the bowls, and the cups: and for the golden basons he gave gold by weight for every bason; and likewise silver by weight for every bason of silver:
And for the altar of incense refined gold by weight; and gold for the pattern of the chariot of the cherubims, that spread out their wings, and covered the ark of the covenant of the Lord.
All this, said David, the Lord made me understand in writing by his hand upon me, even all the works of this pattern.

20.pericope_label: And David said to Solomon his son, Be strong and of good courage, and do it: fear not, nor be dismayed: for the Lord God, even my God, will be with thee; he will not fail thee, nor forsake thee, until thou hast finished all the work for the service of the house of the Lord. And, behold, the courses of the priests and the Levites, even they shall be with thee for all the service of the house of God: and there shall be with thee for all manner of workmanship every willing skilful man, for any manner of service: also the princes and all the people will be wholly at thy commandment.

schools.summary: Ellicott places the words as the resumption of a charge interrupted by the transfer of the plans, presses fail into drop or desert, denies that until says anything about the time beyond it, and reads the behold and the following clause as gestures toward people standing present; Delitzsch refuses that reading, taking the behold to point at the priestly classes as an institution rather than at men in the room, and defends a disputed particle Bertheau wanted deleted.
Gill identifies the courses as the ones David had lately fixed to take their turns in the temple once it was built.

Wesley expands my God into David's commendation of his own experience and draws the conclusion that God never leaves any unless they first leave him; Clarke gives the Targum's substitution of the Word of the Lord for God himself and closes on the father's piety and prudence rather than the son's task.

debates.question: Were the priests and Levites present in the assembly as David spoke?

positions.position: Yes; the form of expression suggests David pointed to them
No; the reference is to the classes as an institution and does not presuppose their presence

outliers.claim: Insists that until thou hast finished implies nothing whatever about the time beyond the stated limit, marking the end of the guarantee and not of the help.

themes: And David said to Solomon his son, Be strong and of good courage, and do it: fear not, nor be dismayed: for the Lord God, even my God, will be with thee; he will not fail thee, nor forsake thee, until thou hast finished all the work for the service of the house of the Lord.

And, behold, the courses of the priests and the Levites, even they shall be with thee for all the service of the house of God: and there shall be with thee for all manner of workmanship every willing skilful man, for any manner of service: also the princes and all the people will be wholly at thy commandment.
